title: Immune Responses in Urinary Disease
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how the immune system injures the kidney and how the urinary tract defends itself. It sorts glomerular disease by mechanism (anti-GBM antibody, immune complexes, or ANCA), shows how serum complement reveals which pathway a disease consumes, and compares the vasculitides by vessel size. It then covers the mechanical and mucosal defenses against urinary infection, immune attack on and escape by renal cell carcinoma, and the serology of hepatitis B vaccination. Board questions usually give an immunofluorescence pattern, a complement result, an ANCA type, or a serology panel and ask for the disease and its mechanism, so the reasoning here is built around those findings.
prerequisites: Glomerular filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane (GBM), podocytes, and mesangium
Hypersensitivity types I to IV and the effector cells of each
Classical, alternative, and lectin complement pathways
Antigen processing on MHC class I and class II and T cell help for B cells

connections.how: The immune mechanisms here explain the light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy findings of each glomerulonephritis.
Goodpasture syndrome, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis link pulmonary hemorrhage or airway granulomas to glomerulonephritis.
IgA vasculitis causes bowel wall hemorrhage and intussusception, and chronic hepatitis B drives membranous nephropathy and polyarteritis nodosa.
Uropathogenic E. coli adhesins defeat urinary defenses, and streptococcal infection triggers poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
VHL-driven renal cell carcinoma illustrates T cell and NK cell surveillance and escape through MHC class I loss and PD-L1.

sections.title: Three immune mechanisms of glomerular injury

blocks.text: The glomerulus is a common target of immune injury because it filters a large plasma volume under high pressure through a charged basement membrane. Three mechanisms account for most immune glomerulonephritis, and each leaves a recognizable immunofluorescence pattern, because the pattern reflects where the antigen sits.
Type II: anti-GBM antibody

In anti-GBM disease, IgG autoantibodies bind the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. This antigen is part of the basement membrane itself and is spread evenly along every capillary loop, so bound IgG, usually with C3, outlines the GBM as a smooth linear ribbon. Antibody binding activates complement and Fc receptor bearing leukocytes, which break capillary walls. Fibrin then leaks into Bowman space, where parietal epithelial cells proliferate and monocytes and macrophages migrate in to form crescents, the lesion of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). The same alpha-3 chain is present in alveolar basement membrane, where the epitope is normally hidden behind intact endothelium. Injury that exposes it, such as smoking, inhaled hydrocarbons, or infection, allows antibody to cause alveolar hemorrhage. Glomerulonephritis plus pulmonary hemorrhage with anti-GBM antibody is Goodpasture syndrome.
Type III: immune complex disease

Immune complexes either circulate and lodge in the glomerulus or form in place when antibody meets an antigen fixed in or planted on the glomerulus. Either way they are discrete clumps, so immunofluorescence is granular. Location shapes the disease. Subendothelial and mesangial deposits face the blood, recruit neutrophils and monocytes, and cause nephritic inflammation, as in lupus nephritis and IgA nephropathy. Subepithelial deposits lie outside the reach of circulating leukocytes; in membranous nephropathy they injure podocytes through the complement membrane attack complex (C5b-9) and cause nephrotic proteinuria with little inflammation. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is nonetheless nephritic: its large subepithelial humps are accompanied by mesangial and subendothelial deposits and an intense neutrophil infiltrate.
Pauci-immune ANCA disease

In ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, autoantibodies activate neutrophils inside glomerular capillaries (mechanism in C03). Neutrophil proteases and oxygen radicals cause necrosis and crescents, yet little immunoglobulin remains, so immunofluorescence is weak or negative. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis are the examples.

blocks.predict: A biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli but only faint, scattered immunoglobulin staining. Which serum test is most likely to be positive, and which is likely negative?
blocks.explain: Weak staining means pauci-immune disease, so ANCA (PR3 or MPO) is the likely positive test. Anti-GBM antibody would give bright linear IgG, and an immune complex disease would give granular deposits.
blocks.check: The immunofluorescence column of the mechanism table.

blocks.text: Serum complement falls when a disease consumes it faster than the liver makes it, and the pattern of C3 and C4 shows which pathway is being used. The classical pathway starts when C1q binds IgG or IgM in immune complexes; C1 cleaves C4 and C2, forming the C3 convertase C4b2a. The alternative pathway bypasses C4: C3b with factor B, cleaved by factor D, forms the C3 convertase C3bBb, stabilized by properdin. Both converge on C3. Classical activation therefore lowers C4 and C3, while alternative activation lowers C3 with normal C4.

In PSGN, nephritogenic streptococcal antigens (such as streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B and a plasmin receptor) form complexes that mainly activate the alternative pathway, so C3 is low and C4 is usually normal. C3 returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks as the antigen is cleared. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) also lowers C3, but it stays low. In the C3 glomerulopathies (including dense deposit disease), C3 nephritic factor or a defect in factor H keeps the alternative pathway running, so C3 falls and C4 stays normal. Immune complex MPGN, often from chronic hepatitis C with cryoglobulins, uses the classical pathway and can lower C4 as well.

Lupus nephritis is driven by IgG complexes of DNA and nucleosomes, so classical pathway consumption lowers both C3 and C4, and levels fall further during flares. Inherited deficiency of C1q, C2, or C4 predisposes to lupus because these proteins help clear apoptotic debris and immune complexes. Immunofluorescence in lupus often shows IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q together, the full house pattern.

IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA vasculitis keep normal serum complement. IgA does not activate the classical pathway, and the local alternative and lectin activation it causes in the mesangium is too small to lower serum levels. Anti-GBM disease and ANCA disease injure the kidney through antibody bound to tissue or activated neutrophils rather than through large circulating complex loads.

blocks.title: Using the timing of C3
blocks.text: A 9-year-old has cola-colored urine, edema, and hypertension 2 weeks after a sore throat. C3 is low, C4 normal, and anti-streptolysin O is raised. The 2-week latency, isolated low C3, and streptococcal serology fit PSGN, and C3 should normalize by about 8 weeks. If C3 is still low at 12 weeks, PSGN no longer explains it. Persistent isolated low C3 with normal C4 suggests continuing alternative pathway activation, as in C3 glomerulopathy with C3 nephritic factor, and biopsy would show MPGN pattern with dominant C3 staining. Had C4 also been low, lupus or immune complex MPGN would be the concern.

Vasculitides are classified by the size of vessel they involve, and vessel size predicts which organs are hit. The ANCA-associated vasculitides affect small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles, and small arteries), so they damage glomeruli and alveolar capillaries. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) affects medium muscular arteries and spares these capillary beds.

ANCA are directed against PR3 or MPO, enzymes normally stored in neutrophil granules. Cytokines such as TNF released during an infection prime neutrophils to move these enzymes to the cell surface. ANCA then bind them and, through Fc receptors, activate the neutrophil to degranulate, produce oxygen radicals, and release neutrophil extracellular traps next to the endothelium. The result is necrotizing vasculitis with few deposits. On indirect immunofluorescence of ethanol-fixed neutrophils, PR3-ANCA gives granular cytoplasmic staining (c-ANCA) and MPO-ANCA stains around the nucleus (p-ANCA), because MPO redistributes during fixation; specific PR3 and MPO immunoassays now confirm the target.

blocks.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) adds necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tract to the vasculitis. Granulomas in the nose and sinuses cause chronic sinusitis, mucosal ulcers, and septal collapse (saddle nose); in the lung they form nodules that may cavitate; the kidney shows focal necrotizing pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis. Most patients with active GPA have PR3-ANCA. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) produces the same necrotizing small vessel vasculitis in kidney and lung, with glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis, but without granulomas and without destructive upper airway disease; it is usually MPO-ANCA positive.

PAN is a transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium and small muscular arteries with fibrinoid necrosis. Lesions are segmental and of different ages in the same patient. Because it spares arterioles, capillaries, and venules, glomerulonephritis and lung involvement are absent and ANCA is negative. Weakening of the renal and interlobar artery walls produces microaneurysms seen on angiography, and narrowing and thrombosis cause renal infarcts and renin-mediated hypertension. About a third of classic cases are linked to chronic hepatitis B, through immune complexes containing viral antigen. Other targets include mesenteric arteries (abdominal pain, bleeding) and the vasa nervorum (mononeuritis multiplex).

blocks.title: GPA, MPA, and PAN compared
rows: Glomeruli spared; microaneurysms, infarcts, renin-driven hypertension
blocks.caption: Glomerulonephritis means small vessel disease; renal artery aneurysms without GN mean medium vessel disease.

blocks.predict: A 45-year-old with hepatitis B has hypertension, abdominal pain after meals, foot drop, and a bland urinalysis. Why is there no glomerulonephritis even though the kidney is involved?
blocks.explain: This is PAN, which inflames medium muscular arteries and spares glomerular capillaries. Renal involvement is ischemic (infarcts and renin release), not glomerular inflammation, so red cell casts are absent.

blocks.text: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood, mostly between about 3 and 15 years of age. It often follows an upper respiratory infection, and it is an immune complex small vessel vasculitis with IgA-dominant deposits in skin, gut, joints, and glomeruli.

The central abnormality is IgA1 with too little galactose on the O-linked sugars of its hinge region. Mucosal infection increases production of this galactose-deficient IgA1, and IgG or IgA autoantibodies recognize the exposed hinge sugars and form complexes. These complexes deposit in small vessel walls and in the glomerular mesangium, activate complement locally through the alternative and lectin pathways, and recruit neutrophils. Serum C3 and C4 stay normal.

steps: Upper respiratory infection stimulates mucosal IgA1
Galactose-deficient IgA1 exposes hinge region sugars

Local complement activation recruits neutrophils
Purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, hematuria
blocks.caption: The same complexes cause the skin, gut, and kidney lesions.

blocks.text: Each manifestation follows from small vessel inflammation. In the skin, leukocytoclastic vasculitis of dermal venules lets red cells escape into an inflamed, edematous dermis, so the purpura is raised and palpable. It concentrates on the buttocks and the extensor surfaces of the legs, where gravity raises venous pressure. Platelet count and coagulation are normal, which separates it from thrombocytopenic purpura. Arthralgia or arthritis, usually of the knees and ankles, is transient and nonerosive. In the gut, vasculitis of the bowel wall causes colicky pain, edema, and bleeding; an edematous or hemorrhagic segment of wall can act as a lead point and telescope into the next segment, so intussusception occurs, often confined to the small bowel.

The kidney lesion is mesangial IgA deposition with mesangial proliferation, identical on biopsy to IgA nephropathy, and it presents with hematuria, sometimes with proteinuria. Most children recover, but renal involvement determines long-term outcome, and adults with IgA vasculitis have more severe kidney disease. IgA nephropathy is best thought of as the kidney-limited form of the same process. A useful timing distinction is that IgA nephropathy causes hematuria within a day or two of a mucosal infection, while PSGN appears 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis.

sections.title: Urinary tract defenses and what defeats them

blocks.text: Above the distal urethra, urine is normally sterile. Most urinary tract infections are ascending: bowel flora such as uropathogenic E. coli colonize the periurethral area, enter the bladder, and may climb the ureter to the kidney. The urinary tract resists this mainly by mechanics, supported by mucosal and innate immune defenses.

The most important defense is flushing. Urine flows one way from kidney to urethra, and the bladder empties almost completely at each void, so bacteria that enter are diluted by new urine and expelled before they can multiply to large numbers. The ureterovesical junction prevents backflow. Each ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall in a submucosal tunnel, so as the bladder fills and during voiding, rising pressure flattens the tunnel against the detrusor and closes it like a flap valve. Ureteral peristalsis also carries urine forward.

Mucosal defenses add to this. A glycosaminoglycan layer coats the urothelium and resists adherence. Uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein), made by the thick ascending limb, binds the type 1 fimbriae of E. coli and carries bacteria out in urine. When bacteria invade superficial umbrella cells, those cells are shed into the urine with their passengers, and the underlying cells regenerate. Urothelial Toll-like receptor 4 detects lipopolysaccharide and triggers IL-8 release, which recruits neutrophils (pyuria), and antimicrobial peptides and secretory IgA limit growth. A short female urethra is one reason infection is more common in women.

blocks.title: How stasis sustains infection
steps: Obstruction or poor emptying leaves residual urine
Bacteria in residual urine multiply between voids
Higher bacterial load overwhelms mucosal defenses
Inflammation and edema further impair drainage
blocks.caption: Any break in flushing lets the bacterial count rise with each cycle.

blocks.text: Each classic risk factor removes a defense. Obstruction from stones, prostatic enlargement, urethral stricture, or posterior urethral valves causes stasis and residual urine above the block, and an obstructed infected kidney cannot clear bacteria. Neurogenic bladder, as in diabetic neuropathy or spinal cord injury, leaves residual urine for the same reason. Vesicoureteral reflux, most often primary from a congenitally short intravesical ureter in children, carries infected bladder urine to the renal pelvis, converting cystitis into pyelonephritis and renal scarring; urine refluxes into the open ducts of compound papillae, which cluster at the poles, so scars favor the poles. An indwelling catheter bypasses the urethra, keeps the bladder neck open, leaves residual urine below the balloon, and becomes coated with biofilm, where bacteria are shielded from flow, antibodies, and neutrophils. In pregnancy, progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle and the enlarging uterus compresses the ureters at the pelvic brim (more on the right), so the upper tracts dilate and drain slowly; asymptomatic bacteriuria therefore progresses to pyelonephritis more often than in nonpregnant women.

blocks.title: Risk factors and the defense each removes
rows: Pyelonephritis and renal scarring in children

blocks.caption: Each risk factor is easiest to remember by the specific defense it breaks.

sections.title: Immune surveillance and escape in renal cell carcinoma

blocks.text: Renal cell carcinoma, most often the clear cell type driven by VHL loss, is usually heavily infiltrated by T cells and is regarded as an immunogenic tumor. It illustrates the two arms of antitumor immunity, CD8+ T cells and NK cells, and the ways tumors escape both.

Every nucleated cell displays fragments of its own proteins on MHC class I. Cytosolic proteins are degraded by the proteasome, the peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP, loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2 microglobulin, and carried to the surface. Tumor cells present abnormal peptides this way: mutated proteins (neoantigens) and normal proteins that are overexpressed or reexpressed. Naive CD8+ T cells are first activated in lymph nodes by dendritic cells that take up tumor material and cross-present it on class I, with costimulation through CD28 and B7. Activated cytotoxic T cells then recognize the same peptide and class I complex on the tumor through the T cell receptor, with CD8 binding the class I molecule, and kill by perforin and granzymes and by Fas ligand. Their interferon-gamma raises class I expression on nearby tumor cells.

NK cells need no prior sensitization. Their inhibitory receptors (killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptors and CD94/NKG2A) recognize self MHC class I and block killing. A cell that loses class I removes this brake, and if it also displays stress ligands such as MICA and MICB for the activating receptor NKG2D, the NK cell kills it with perforin and granzymes. NK cells also kill antibody-coated cells through CD16 (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity).

Tumors escape by turning these mechanisms against themselves. Mutation or silencing of HLA genes, beta-2 microglobulin, or TAP lowers class I and hides tumor peptides from CD8+ T cells. That should invite NK cell attack, which tumors avoid by shedding NKG2D ligands or by an immunosuppressive environment. Tumor cells and infiltrating myeloid cells also express PD-L1, often induced by interferon-gamma from the very T cells attacking them. PD-L1 binds PD-1 on activated T cells, recruits phosphatases that damp T cell receptor and CD28 signaling, and drives T cell exhaustion. Regulatory T cells, TGF-beta, and VEGF, which is overproduced in VHL-deficient tumors and impairs dendritic cell maturation, add further suppression. Antibodies that block PD-1 or PD-L1 work by removing this brake, which is the mechanistic basis of checkpoint inhibition.

blocks.caption: Losing MHC class I trades T cell attack for NK cell attack, so successful tumors usually need more than one escape route.

blocks.predict: A tumor clone acquires a beta-2 microglobulin mutation. Which effector cell loses the ability to kill it, and which gains it?
blocks.explain: Without beta-2 microglobulin, MHC class I cannot reach the surface, so CD8+ T cells can no longer recognize tumor peptide. NK cell inhibitory receptors are no longer engaged, so NK cells can kill the clone if activating ligands are present.

sections.title: Hepatitis B vaccination and membranous nephropathy

blocks.text: The hepatitis B vaccine contains recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) produced in yeast and adsorbed to an aluminum adjuvant. HBsAg self-assembles into virus-like particles that carry the antigen in repeated arrays but contain no viral DNA and no core protein, so they cannot cause infection.

Because HBsAg is a protein, the response is T cell dependent. Dendritic cells take up the particles, present HBsAg peptides on MHC class II, and activate CD4+ helper T cells. B cells whose receptors bind HBsAg internalize it, present peptides to these helper cells, and receive CD40 ligand and cytokine signals. In germinal centers the B cells switch from IgM to IgG and undergo affinity maturation, producing long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells. The resulting antibody, anti-HBs, binds the surface antigen on the viral envelope and neutralizes the virus before it can infect hepatocytes. A titer of at least 10 mIU/mL after the full series is regarded as protective.

steps: Recombinant HBsAg particles with alum adjuvant
Dendritic cells present HBsAg on MHC class II
CD4+ helper T cells activated
HBsAg-specific B cells receive CD40L and cytokines

Plasma cells secrete anti-HBs; memory B cells persist
blocks.caption: A protein antigen with T cell help produces durable, high-affinity IgG.

blocks.text: Serology separates vaccination from infection because the vaccine contains only surface antigen. Natural infection exposes the immune system to the whole virus, including core antigen, so it produces anti-HBc. A vaccinated person makes anti-HBs but never anti-HBc. Anti-HBs with anti-HBc means recovery from past infection, and HBsAg with anti-HBc means current infection.

blocks.title: Hepatitis B serology patterns
blocks.caption: Anti-HBc is the marker of exposure to the virus; anti-HBs alone is the vaccine signature.

blocks.text: Chronic hepatitis B causes membranous nephropathy, most often in children in endemic regions. Viral antigens, especially HBeAg, reach the glomerulus and combine with antibody in the subepithelial space, forming granular IgG and C3 deposits. Because these deposits lie outside the reach of circulating leukocytes, injury comes from complement membrane attack complexes damaging podocytes, which causes nephrotic proteinuria with little inflammation. Unlike primary membranous nephropathy, this secondary form usually lacks antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor. Preventing infection removes the antigen source, and in regions with universal infant vaccination, hepatitis B associated membranous nephropathy in children has declined.

blocks.title: Reading a hepatitis B panel
blocks.text: A nursing student has HBsAg negative, anti-HBs 85 mIU/mL, and anti-HBc negative. HBsAg negative excludes current infection. Anti-HBs above 10 mIU/mL shows protective antibody. Anti-HBc negative shows the immune system has never seen core antigen, so the antibody did not come from infection; this is vaccine immunity. A classmate has HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, and anti-HBc positive. The same anti-HBs now sits beside anti-HBc, so this is immunity after a resolved natural infection. A third student positive only for anti-HBc needs further testing, since this pattern can mean the window period, remote infection with waning anti-HBs, or a false positive.

integration.text: Anatomy and immunology together explain where immune disease strikes. The type IV collagen alpha-3 chain shared by glomerular and alveolar basement membranes links the kidney and lung in Goodpasture syndrome, and the capillary beds of the glomerulus and alveolus explain why small vessel ANCA vasculitis produces pulmonary-renal syndromes while medium vessel PAN spares both. Serum complement then separates classical from alternative pathway disease. Neither test stands alone, because complement can be normal early in lupus and ANCA can be negative in a minority of pauci-immune disease, so biopsy immunofluorescence remains the reference.

Microbiology runs through the chapter. Streptococcal and respiratory infections trigger PSGN and IgA disease, hepatitis B supplies the antigen for membranous nephropathy and PAN, and E. coli adhesins test urinary defenses that are mostly mechanical, so anatomy and urodynamics are the main predictors of infection risk. Renal cell carcinoma shows that the same MHC class I pathway that presents viral peptides also presents tumor peptides, and that tumors survive by the same inhibitory checkpoints that normally prevent immune damage to healthy tissue.

summary: Linear IgG along the GBM is type II anti-GBM disease (alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen); with lung hemorrhage it is Goodpasture syndrome.
Granular deposits are type III immune complex disease (PSGN, lupus, IgA nephropathy, membranous); little or no staining is pauci-immune ANCA disease.
Subendothelial and mesangial deposits cause nephritic inflammation; subepithelial deposits injure podocytes through C5b-9 and cause nephrotic proteinuria.
Low C3 with normal C4 means alternative pathway activation (PSGN, C3 glomerulopathy); low C3 and C4 means classical pathway activation (lupus).
PSGN C3 normalizes by about 8 weeks; persistently low C3 suggests MPGN. IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA vasculitis keep normal complement.
GPA is PR3-ANCA with airway granulomas and GN; MPA is MPO-ANCA with GN and capillaritis but no granulomas; PAN is ANCA negative, spares glomeruli, and causes renal microaneurysms.
IgA vasculitis follows respiratory infection in children and causes palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, intussusception, and mesangial IgA GN with normal platelets.
Flushing by one-way flow, complete emptying, and the flap-valve ureterovesical junction is the main urinary defense; obstruction, reflux, catheters, and pregnancy each break it.
CD8+ T cells kill tumor cells presenting peptide on MHC class I; NK cells kill cells missing class I; tumors escape by losing class I and expressing PD-L1.
Anti-HBs alone is vaccine immunity because the vaccine contains only HBsAg; preventing hepatitis B prevents its membranous nephropathy.

verify: Percentages of ANCA positivity (PR3 in most active GPA, MPO in most MPA) and the about one-third hepatitis B association of classic PAN vary between sources and have changed as hepatitis B vaccination spread; confirm the figures NABNE expects.
The time for C3 to normalize after PSGN is given as 6 to 8 weeks in most texts and up to 12 weeks in some; confirm the cutoff NABNE uses to suggest MPGN.
MPGN classification has moved from types I, II, and III to immune complex MPGN versus C3 glomerulopathy; confirm which terminology NABNE Part I uses.

Confirm whether NABNE uses the newer names IgA vasculitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis or the eponyms Henoch-Schonlein purpura, Wegener granulomatosis, and Churg-Strauss syndrome.
The age range for IgA vasculitis (about 3 to 15 years) and the statement that its intussusception is often confined to the small bowel come from pediatric sources and vary in detail.
The protective anti-HBs threshold of 10 mIU/mL is a public health consensus value; confirm it is the value NABNE tests.

The specific streptococcal nephritogenic antigens (streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B and nephritis-associated plasmin receptor) and whether PSGN also uses the lectin pathway are still discussed in the literature.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: glomerular-if-patterns (linear, granular, and pauci-immune immunofluorescence side by side with deposit locations) and ureterovesical-junction (oblique intramural ureter acting as a flap valve).
